title: Awenji, the Twin Stones
subtitle: Two Hands Beneath One Weight

lore.description:
Awenji are twin spirits — one of stone, one of gear — who dance together to keep the walking cities of Ngomebe alive. They were not born; they were carved. The first stone city needed a keystone and a bearing, and the first Mason-Kin and the first Aeler vent-prior worked together for nine years to make them fit. When the city walked, the two spirits emerged from the joint — one from the stone, one from the gear — still holding hands. They teach that no craft is complete without another, that a bridge needs two shores, and that the strongest keystone is the one that bears the weight of a partner's trust.

**Who stands beside the twins.**

Ngomebe depictions usually leave the joint between Awenji visible. One image is worked in stone and the other carries metal that can be removed for repair. The pair belongs to the people maintaining it. At a new workshop, the maker of the socket and the maker of the moving part stand together while each explains what the other made possible. An apprentice may do the explaining if the masters are unable to attend. Some Houses find that allowance inconveniently generous.

The account of the first Mason-Kin and vent-prior working for nine years remains the cult's central history. Later workshops disagree over what to imitate. One prizes the years of patience; another the moment two traditions abandoned incompatible measurements. Each can point to a functioning machine as evidence, and neither is entitled to claim the other people's invention as its own.

**The lintels of the Mountain Satrapies.**

The Twin Keystone devotion reached Aeler-Dhaharan workplaces with traveling carvers and engineers. Its lintels became common where the owner of a mine and the people supplying its bearings could each halt the other's work. Older examples show hands of equal size. Later patrons have sometimes had one enlarged and the other recut as an assistant's. A returning craft family can date a change in authority by finding its own chisel marks beneath the alteration.

This movement of a cult does not make Ngomebe's Aeler immigrants from the Himadri. A design, a song, and a household can travel by different routes. Satrapy worshippers have added local mountain manners to the paired ceremony; Ngomebe visitors notice when silence replaces the repair crews' customary argument over which part failed first.

**The carrier is also in the room.**

The Walking City's Weight has forced a question the workshop rite once passed over. Stone and bearing can fit perfectly while the living carrier below them comes from the same few Sledge-Born families. Those families have begun bringing the carrier's feeding bowl to ceremonies that otherwise display only the tools of masons and engineers. They do not propose a third spirit. They ask why partnership is being celebrated without naming everyone who sustains it.

Some keepers welcome the bowl and speak the carrier's name before the makers'. Others fear that every Naming will become a confrontation they cannot resolve without stopping the city. Neither the genuine honor of carrying nor the reality of unequal service disappears because Awenji's image is balanced.

In mixed foothill communities the twins also attend marriages and household partnerships. The local rite asks each person to describe work the other should never have to do alone. It makes no promise that the work will divide evenly. A dispute over who may stand beside the twins can bring engineers, carriers' relatives, and a household awaiting its wedding into the same meeting, with substantially different reasons to care about the result.
lore.followers: Among the peoples of Fate's Edge, Awenji are invoked by masons, engineers, and any two people who must work in perfect trust. In the Mountain Satrapies, they are carved on the lintels of Aeler-Dhaharan counting-houses. In Ngomebe, they are painted on the rollers of every new city. Wherever a stone is set by one hand and sealed by another, Awenji dance.
lore.quote: Awenji taught us that a single stone is just a rock. Two stones, set together, can hold back a river. One gear is a toy. Two gears can move a city. Find your twin. Work. Do not let go.

domain_focus: Partnership: two hands, two crafts, two wills working as one
Balance: equal weight, equal credit, equal sacrifice
The Union of Aeler and Ngomebe: stone and gear, mountain and plateau
The Twin Keystone: the joint that bears the load; break one, and both fall

thiasos.description: Awenji's Thiasos is always a matched pair: twin mice that sleep curled together, two lizards that change color in synchrony, two beetles that share the same burden, or two gray doves that answer each other's calls from opposite sides of a room.
thiasos.care: The pair needs ordinary care and must remain together. If separated for more than a day, both become Compromised: they grow listless, and their Runekeeper suffers –1 die on rolls involving coordination or assistance until they are reunited.

codex.description: A Codex sworn to Awenji is never a book written by one hand. It may be a pair of matched slate tablets, each inscribed with half of every Rite; a single scroll that must be held by two people to be read; a set of twin bells that ring only when struck together; or a keystone with two faces, each carved by a different mason.
codex.upkeep: Because Awenji's truths are written in duality, the Codex requires upkeep: the Runekeeper must spend an hour each week with a partner (any willing person), reading each Rite aloud together, or the words become mismatched (treat as Compromised until re-paired).

patrons_gift.name: Awenji's Union
patrons_gift.description: Once per scene as an action, a Runekeeper of Awenji may touch two held items (weapons, tools, or pieces of armor) and whisper a word of union.
patrons_gift.effect: For the rest of the scene, each item grants +1 die to rolls made to assist the other bearer, and the first time each scene the two bearers would be separated by force (a closing door, a collapsing floor, a spell of banishment), they may reroll the resistance check (the twin stones hold).
patrons_gift.cost: After the scene, each user marks +1 Obligation to Awenji.

rites.name: Rite of the Balanced Weight
rites.materials: Two stones of equal weight, or a single gear that has been split and re-joined.
rites.effect: You and an ally within Near gain +1 die to any roll made to assist each other for the scene. When one of you takes the Assist action, the other gains an additional +1 die (stacking with the normal assist bonus).
rites.push_it: The bond is visible — a faint line of golden light connects you. Any enemy who sees it must test Resolve (DV 3) or be unable to target only one of you; they must attack both or neither. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Twin Bearing
rites.materials: A pair of matched tools, or a shared handhold on a single object.
rites.effect: You and an ally lifting, carrying, or crafting the same object together treat it as if it weighed half as much, and gain +1 die to any Craft or Body roll made jointly on it for the scene.
rites.push_it: Extend the effect to a third and fourth pair of hands working the same task, so long as all are within Near range. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of Awenji's Seal
rites.materials: Two objects that belong to two different people (a ring, a lock of hair, a personal seal).
rites.effect: Touch two objects; for one day, they cannot be separated by less than magical force. If one is moved, the other moves with it. This can be used to lock a door (the door and its frame), to bind a prisoner's hands (left and right manacle), or to keep two allies from being pulled apart by a trap.
rites.push_it: The seal is permanent until broken by a ritual of separation (requiring the consent of both parties). Mark +2 Obligation. If one party breaks the seal by force, they suffer 2 Harm (spiritual backlash). Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Shared Cornerstone
rites.materials: A keystone or capstone fragment, split evenly between two partners.
rites.effect: You and a bonded partner each gain +1 Effect on rolls to defend the other from harm, and once per scene, one of you may intercept an attack meant for the other, treating the Harm as if it were one level lower.
rites.push_it: Fully absorb one instance of Harm meant for your partner, taking it as your own at full severity. Mark 1 SB (Spades). Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Dance of Stone
rites.materials: A keystone chip from a walking city, and a gear from an Aeler bearing.
rites.effect: You and an ally may move a stone city's roller 1 mile without oxen — but you both mark 2 Fatigue. The city will remember your aid; the Mason-Kin will grant you a Keystone Charter (right to dwell in any Ngomebe city for a season) if you succeed. If you fail, the roller cracks, and the city stops until a Mason-Kin can repair it.
rites.push_it: Move the roller 2 miles instead of 1. Mark +3 Obligation and both you and your ally gain a permanent scar — a crack on your palm that never heals, matching the crack in the roller. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +4) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

cantors.name: The Cantor's Song
cantors.description: A Cantor of Awenji sings in duets — melodies that require two voices to complete. One voice begins a phrase; the other finishes it. A Cantor alone can only hum half a tune. Their voice is used to synchronize work crews, to heal the rift between feuding partners, or to remind two people that they were once one team. Awenji's Cantors are often found on construction sites, in counting-houses where two clerks share a ledger, or at weddings where they sing the vows as a round.

cult.name: The Cult of the Twin Keystone
cult.description: Awenji's cults meet in pairs — literally. Each member must bring a partner. The Twin Keystone is a fellowship of masons, engineers, and Aeler-Dhaharan families who have intermarried. A ritual involves each pair carving a single rune on a shared stone — one carves the left half, the other the right. If the rune is complete, the stone is added to a growing cairn. If it is mismatched, the pair must spend a day working together before they may try again. Their creed is carved on a single stone that is never split: "One stone is a rock. Two stones are a foundation. A foundation holds the world." Outsiders are welcome if they bring a partner. If they come alone, they will be given a partner — and the partner may not be human.

witchcraft.name: The Art of the Joint-Smith
witchcraft.description: A witch who walks with Awenji is a joint-smith or bond-weaver — one who crafts the places where two things meet. Their magic works through the tools of union: a double-headed hammer that strikes two nails at once, a pair of tongs that cannot be separated by less than a forge's heat, or a spirit level that has two bubbles — one for each partner. Their tools are never single; a hammer without a matching pair is just a club.
witchcraft.lore: Joint-smiths often work in pairs themselves, apprenticed to Awenji in twos so they might understand from the outset that their craft cannot be practiced alone. They are called to mend broken marriages of stone as often as broken marriages of people, and many carry both a mason's hammer and a peacemaker's patience in the same satchel.
witchcraft.quote: A hammer without a matching pair is just a club.

twin_needles.name: The Twin Needles
twin_needles.description: Two needles of cold iron, bound by a single thread that never tangles. Once per session, the witch may sew two objects together (two pages of a contract, two door handles, two sleeves of a shirt). For the next day, they cannot be separated without the witch's consent. Cutting the thread causes both objects to rust instantly. The needles can also be used to stitch a wound closed; the patient and the healer share the pain (each takes 1 Fatigue, but the wound heals 1 Harm).

hedge_gifts.name: Shared Breath
hedge_gifts.description: Once per scene, you and an ally within Near may each spend 1 Boon to share a single breath. For the rest of the scene, whenever one of you rolls a 1, the other may take that Story Beat instead of the GM (the GM does not gain it). The beat must be spent on a complication that affects the character who took it.

hedge_gifts.name: Matched Grip
hedge_gifts.description: Once per scene, you and a partner working the same tool or weapon together gain +1 die to any roll made using it, as long as you remain in Touch range of each other.

hedge_gifts.name: The Level's Bubble
hedge_gifts.description: Passive. You can always tell, by touch alone, whether a structure, joint, or agreement is truly balanced or secretly favors one side.

hedge_gifts.name: Cornerstone's Patience
hedge_gifts.description: Once per session, you may spend an extended scene helping to mend a rift between two feuding parties (people or peoples). If both parties genuinely participate, they gain +1 die to their next cooperative roll together.

monastic_tradition.name: The Way of the Twin Keystone
monastic_tradition.description: Monks of the Twin Keystone are never ordained alone; the order requires each initiate to be paired with a partner before their first vow is spoken, and the two train, fight, and advance together for the rest of their lives. Their forms are built around two bodies moving as one — strikes that only land because a partner has drawn the enemy's guard, blocks that only hold because a partner braces the other side. A monk of the Twin Keystone who loses their partner does not simply grieve; they must undergo a rite of re-pairing before they can advance further, for the tradition holds that mastery achieved alone is only half a craft.
monastic_tradition.quote: One stone is a rock. Two stones are a foundation.
monastic_tradition.prerequisites: Body 3+, Spirit 2+, Rite of the Balanced Weight or Cantor of Awenji, and a bonded partner (PC or significant NPC).
monastic_tradition.debt_resistant_frame: A debt owed by one is shared by two, and a burden shared is a burden halved. Monks of the Twin Keystone gain +1 die to resist any magical debt, geas, or contract when acting alongside their bonded partner (once per scene). If they succeed, the debt's weight visibly splits and settles evenly across both — easier for either to bear, harder for any creditor to collect in full.

basic.name: Twinned Strike
basic.description: When you and your bonded partner both attack the same target in the same exchange, both gain +1 die to the attack roll, and if both hit, the target's defenses falter, granting +1 Effect to the second attack to land.

advanced.name: Shared Stance
advanced.description: Once per scene, you and your bonded partner may switch positions instantly (swap places anywhere within Near range) as a free action, useful for protecting each other or repositioning mid-combat.

master.name: Avatar of the Twin Stones
master.description: Once per session, you and your bonded partner may act on the same turn, sharing a single pool of actions (one Action each, but you may move as one). After the scene, you both gain a permanent Debt Scar (a faint crack, like dried clay, that appears on the same spot on each of your bodies) but gain +1 die on all future rolls made to assist one another.
master.cost: 2 Fatigue (shared, 1 each) and +1 Obligation to Awenji (shared, 1 each)

monastic_tradition.corruption_note: Monks follow the patron's general Corruption track; the monastic path does not add a second one. Where a tradition needs its own, it must differ from the general track in kind, not degree.

corruption.benefit: Steady Hand: +1 die to Craft rolls when working with a partner.
corruption.cost: Partner-Dependent: –1 die to any Craft roll made alone.

corruption.benefit: Twin's Instinct: Once per scene, you may know the emotional state of your bonded partner without speaking.
corruption.cost: Shared Pain: When your partner takes Harm, you must test Resolve (DV 3) or mark 1 Fatigue.

corruption.benefit: Two as One: +2 dice to assists, and the first assist each scene does not cost a Boon.
corruption.cost: Jealous Joint: –1 die to social rolls with anyone your partner distrusts.

corruption.benefit: Unbreakable Seal: Once per session, declare a bond between two objects or people; it cannot be broken by non-magical means for one week.
corruption.cost: Compulsive Union: You must try to reconcile any two arguing parties you witness; ignoring a quarrel costs 1 Fatigue.

corruption.benefit: Dance of Stone: Once per session, you and a partner may move a massive object as if it weighed nothing — but you both mark 1 Fatigue.
corruption.cost: Cracked Keystone: Each use causes a visible crack to appear on your skin. After nine cracks, you cannot be separated from your partner by any means, but you also cannot leave their side.

corruption.benefit: Avatar of the Twin Stones: Once per session, you and a bonded partner may act on the same turn, sharing a single pool of actions.
corruption.cost: Twin's Doom: Mark +3 Obligation. If one of you dies, the other must test Resolve (DV 5) or fall catatonic for 1d4 days. Your reflections now always appear in pairs, even when you are alone.

playstyle_notes.description: Build scenes around two characters trusting each other with different parts of the same job. Awenji's gifts support cooperation; their corruption makes working alone increasingly difficult. A repair, a disagreement over credit, or a partner who must leave gives that dependence something concrete to test. Partnership need not be romantic or permanent to matter.
emphasizes: Partnership: two hands, two crafts, two wills as one
Balance: equal weight, equal credit, equal sacrifice
Union of Aeler and Ngomebe: stone and gear, mountain and plateau
The Twin Keystone: the joint that bears the load; break one, and both fall

sample_adventure.title: The Cracked Roller
sample_adventure.description: A walking city's central roller has cracked mid-stride, stranding thousands and threatening to collapse the district it carries. The Mason-Kin who first built the roller has died, leaving no partner to complete the repair rite — Awenji's craft requires two hands from two different traditions working as one. The party must find (or become) an unlikely pair capable of finishing what was left half-done, before the city's slow grinding halt turns into a catastrophic fall.
sample_adventure.quote: The roller does not care who fixes it, mason or stranger, kin or foreigner. It asks only that two hands work as one. Find your twin. Do not let go.

guises.name: The Joined Ones
guises.note: On household carvings the stone twin is larger; the gear twin reaches upward to take its hand. Bearing-makers sometimes reverse the proportions. Both versions are admitted at a joint dedication, though old masters inspect which one has been placed over the principal doorway. A ceremony celebrating equality can reveal exactly where the partners think it ends.

guises.among: Akilan Aeler engineers and mixed foothill communities
guises.name: The Two Who Made Room
guises.note: The first offering is an empty place on the bench, kept for the other craft. Families say the founding vent-prior came down because the work required company. Accounts disagree about the home range. No Himadri origin follows from the title vent-prior, and nobody needs to become an Edgewalker or Mason to belong to a household that keeps this practice.

guises.name: The Paired Lintel
guises.note: Carved twins entered Aeler-Dhaharan workshops with traveling artisans and became common above shared premises. Some houses interpreted the joined hands as a warrant for equal testimony; others displayed them above doors through which one partner's workers could enter only by permission. Local disputes turn on whether the image witnesses cooperation or sanctifies an existing arrangement.

guises.name: The Fitting Hands
guises.note: Repair crews have adopted paired marks on gates assembled by different crafts. An Izinyanga's visitor may recognize the twins while hearing unfamiliar songs about water instead of rollers. These shrines are maintained by workshops rather than imposed as a district cult. A canal-mother can respect the dedication and still require the gate to open when the district needs it.

provenance.origin: Ngomebe's founding account: the first Mason-Kin and the first Aeler vent-prior labored together until keystone and bearing fitted, and the twins emerged holding hands.
provenance.summary: Neither craft tells the founding labor in quite the same order. Mason-Kin recitations begin with stone finding its shape; Aeler versions begin with the gear that made movement possible. Roller crews know a verse in which neither craft could hear the other over the work. These differences do not change the established account of a shared origin. They disclose which labor a later household wants honored first.
provenance.the_migration: Artisans carried the twins into the Mountain Satrapies, where a joint workshop had to speak across Aeler and Dhaharan practices. The image proved portable because a lintel could display a partnership before either community agreed how to describe it. Returned apprentices brought altered songs home to Ngomebe. Elders sometimes rejected a supposedly foreign verse that their grandparents had themselves taken abroad.
provenance.why_it_took: Joint dedications now cover arrangements as different as a pair of craftspeople, an extended household, and a workshop employing many people. None is necessarily a marriage. The habit of depicting only two hands can conceal how many others support the undertaking. In Ngomebe, attendants of the living carrier have begun asking where the person carrying the city stands in a picture that shows only the cutter and the engineer.
provenance.note: The question does not abolish the twins' achievement or solve the Weight. The cooperation is real, and so is the repeated absence of the carving Houses from the chamber. Awenji's devotees disagree over whether a third place at the dedication repairs that omission or merely gives it a more attractive ceremony.

philosophy.name: Neither Complete Alone
philosophy.summary: Awenji join unlike work. Their lesson requires both partners to remain capable of disagreeing about the fit.
philosophy.the_point: Trust becomes dependence without recourse when one side alone may declare the joint sound. Declaring every disagreement disloyal destroys the very second judgment that made the collaboration valuable.
philosophy.the_third_thing: The difficult third question is who bears the failure. Two masters can reach an honest agreement while passing the danger to a crew or carrier who was never invited to the bench.
philosophy.at_the_table: Present a collaboration both principals genuinely want to preserve. Let evidence come from the people who operate what they built. Success can improve the partnership without proving that either craft secretly supplied all the knowledge.
